title: Genesis 18. The Cup of Hospitality.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 18. The Cup of Hospitality.
The Lord appeared to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre,
as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day.
Abraham lifts up his eyes.
Three men are standing near him.
He does not recognize them.
He does not ask their names.
He runs to meet them from the tent door,
bows to the ground, and says: My lord,
if I have found favor in your sight,
do not pass by Your servant.
Let water be brought.
Wash your feet.
Rest under the tree.
I will bring bread.
Refresh your hearts.
Then you may go on your way.
The Cup of hospitality.
Abraham serves.
He hurries to the tent: Sarah, quickly, three seahs of fine flour,
knead it, make cakes.
He runs to the herd, takes a tender, good calf,
gives it to a servant, hurries to prepare it.
He takes curds and milk and the calf and sets it before them.
He stands by them under the tree while they eat.
The text moves between "they" and "the Lord" without warning.
Abraham addresses three men.
The Lord speaks.
The shift is not explained.
The line between hosting strangers and hosting God is erased.
The Cup that was carried through fire and smoke in chapter fifteen,
that was sealed in flesh in chapter seventeen,
is now sitting under a tree eating curds and milk prepared by the hands of the man it was given to.
They ask: Where is Sarah your wife?
In the tent.
One says:
I will surely return to you about this time next year,
and Sarah your wife shall have a son.
Sarah is listening at the tent door, behind Him.
Abraham and Sarah are old, advanced in days.
The way of women has ceased to be with Sarah.
The body that was renamed for a mother of nations has stopped being able to become one.
Sarah laughs within herself.
After I am worn out, shall I have pleasure,
and my lord old also?
The same laughter Abraham laughed in chapter seventeen.
The same impossibility.
The same gap between what was promised and what the body can do.
But where Abraham laughed in his heart before God and was answered with a name,
Sarah laughs inside herself behind a tent flap and is answered with a question.
The Lord says to Abraham: Why did Sarah laugh?
Will I really bear a child, now that I am old?
Is anything too hard for the Lord?
At the set time I will return to you,
when the season comes around, and Sarah shall have a son.
God heard what Sarah said to herself.
Inside a tent.
Behind a flap.
In the privacy of her own thoughts.
The Cup of hospitality is also the Cup of exposure.
What is whispered inside a tent is heard by the One sitting under the tree.
You can laugh where no one can see you.
But God hears.
Sarah denies it.
I did not laugh.
She was afraid.
He says: No.
You did laugh.
The same God who let Abraham name his laughter in chapter seventeen now names Sarah's laughter in chapter eighteen.
The son called Laughter, Isaac,
is promised in a moment where both his parents laughed at the idea that he could exist.
The Cup that carries the promise of a son named Laughter was met with laughter by both the father and the mother.
Neither believed.
Both were answered anyway.
The men rise.
They look toward Sodom.
Abraham walks with them to send them on their way.
Then the Lord speaks, not to Abraham, but to Himself:
Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?
Since Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation,
and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him?
For I have known him,
to the end that he may command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord,
to do righteousness and justice,
so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham what He has spoken of him.
God decides to tell Abraham what is coming.
Not because Abraham needs to know,
because Abraham is the one who will teach his children justice.
The Cup that was given to a man without children is now explained to that man in terms of what his children must learn.
The covenant has a purpose beyond offspring and land.
It has a way.
Righteousness and justice.
The nations will be blessed not only through Abraham's seed but through what his household keeps.
The Lord says: The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah is great.
Their sin is very grievous.
I will go down and see whether what has come to Me is as bad as the report.
If not, I will know.
The two men turn toward Sodom.
But Abraham still stood before the Lord.
Abraham drew near.
Will You indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?
Suppose there are fifty righteous within the city.
Will You destroy and not spare the place for the fifty righteous who are in it?
Far be it from You to do such a thing,
to kill the righteous with the wicked,
so that the righteous is like the wicked!
Far be it from You!
Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?
The Cup of intercession.
Abraham stands between God and the city.
The man who received the promise now asks God to apply justice to the promise's neighbors.
Not for the wicked, for the righteous.
The question is not mercy against justice.
It is justice inside justice:
will You destroy the righteous with the wicked?
The Lord says: If I find fifty righteous in Sodom,
I will spare the whole place for their sake.
Abraham, who has called himself dust and ashes, pushes.
What if five of the fifty are lacking?
Will You destroy the city for five?
I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there.
Forty?
I will not do it for the forty.
Thirty?
I will not do it if I find thirty.
Twenty?
I will not destroy it for the twenty.
Let me speak once more.
What if ten are found there?
I will not destroy it for the ten's sake.
The Lord went His way when He had finished speaking with Abraham.
Abraham returned to his place.
The Cup of hospitality held God at a table.
The Cup of intercession held God in a conversation.
Abraham fed God bread and calf and curds.
Then he stood before God and asked Him to be just,
not only to the covenant people but to a city whose men were wicked,
great sinners against the Lord.
The man who gave away his wife, who laughed at the promise,
who tried to substitute Ishmael for Isaac,
this man stood before the Judge of all the earth and asked Him to spare a city for the sake of ten righteous people.
The answer God gave to each question was yes.
Fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten, yes, yes, yes, yes, yes, yes.
The Judge of all the earth agreed to do what is just at every number Abraham named.
The Cup of intercession was not refused.
But Abraham stopped at ten.
He did not go lower.
He did not ask for five.
He did not ask for one.
The man who bargained down from fifty to ten stopped.
And God went His way.
What Abraham did not know, and what the next chapter will show,
is whether ten were found.
The Cup of intercession was poured out.
The question was asked.
The answer was given.
But the city still stands.
And the two men are already walking toward it.
